routes.description: Establish that the earliest recoverable traditions and independent attestations are better explained by a mortal Jewish teacher whose life and teachings were rapidly transformed through scriptural, epic, theological, and communal mythmaking.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by grounding Jesus in early independent tradition, explaining Pauline silence without positing an exclusively celestial Christ, defending external or interpersonal attestation, and showing that extensive Gospel invention remains compatible with an underlying historical person.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving early-source evidence to a first-century Jewish teacher whose subsequent mythologization does not erase his historical existence.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early tradition independent of Gospel literary invention that presents Jesus as a mortal Jewish teacher concerned with law and God's kingdom.
Explain Paul's sparse earthly biography through the purposes of his letters while identifying traditions or relationships that connect Paul to an earthly Jesus movement.
Defend Josephus's James reference and related early testimony as evidence independently anchoring Jesus and his followers in history.
Show how extensive literary and theological transformation can elevate and obscure a historical teacher without requiring that the earthly figure was invented.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for variations in kingdom, Torah, and mission traditions through changing communities and social identities.
Show that shared historical tradition explains the relevant overlaps and developments without unnecessary dependence on wholesale literary reification.

routes.description: Establish that the earliest evidence is more expected if Christianity began with a revelatory Christ and that later authors placed this figure into an earthly story through scriptural and literary reification unsupported by secure independent corroboration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that Paul lacks expected traces of a recent earthly teacher, supplying a coherent revelatory and celestial origin model, explaining Gospel biography as later literary construction, and defeating purported independent attestations or demonstrations that the evidence discriminates in favor of historicity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidentiary pattern of early revelation and later historicization to the proposition that Christianity began without a recent earthly founder.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's repeated reliance on revelation and scripture, together with missing expected earthly references, differentially supports a revelatory-Christ origin.
Provide a historically coherent account in which an incarnate Christ is killed by supernatural powers and known to apostles through revelation.
Explain earthly Gospel narratives as literary transformations of Pauline, scriptural, communal, or revelatory materials rather than memories of a teacher.
Show that Josephus, kinship language, eyewitness claims, and later Christian texts do not securely provide independent attestation of a historical Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require contextual evidence that distinguishes historical-memory explanations from revelatory or literary-reification alternatives.
Constrain reconstruction according to the chronology, dependence, ambiguity, and scarcity of the surviving sources.

sections.title: Paul, revelation, and traces of an earthly life
sections.rationale: Paul is the earliest major evidence in dispute, and the competing explanations of his biographical omissions, revealed knowledge, teachings, and personal contacts directly distinguish the two origin models.

sections.title: Q, Jewish teaching, and kingdom traditions
sections.rationale: The status and independence of traditions about Torah reform, mission, apocalypse, and God's kingdom determine whether an early mortal teacher is recoverable before later Gospel composition.

sections.title: Gospel mythmaking and literary reification
sections.rationale: Both routes must explain how earthly narratives arose, including whether epic and scriptural transformation presupposes a historical subject or can manufacture one from prior revelatory and communal material.

sections.title: Josephus, James, and independent attestation
sections.rationale: The identification of James, the meaning and transmission of the kinship wording, and the legal context determine whether the debate has significant external evidence for Jesus.

sections.title: Later testimony, alternative Christians, and evidential method
sections.rationale: Johannine, Papian, Ignatian, Petrine, and Acts traditions test competing claims about eyewitness memory and early dissent, while comparative standards govern what these sparse sources can establish.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The earliest Christian literature presents Jesus through revelation and does not clearly place him in recent earthly history.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Carrier the opening, and the uninterrupted first-person presentation remains his throughout this window.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the foundational Pauline-silence observation for the revelatory-Christ route and therefore requires no opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances a central route premise using a concrete Pauline example, though the excerpt only begins its demonstration.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording leaves room for uncertainty, but the universal-sounding claim about what the earliest literature discusses exceeds the representative support shown here.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span presents a positive reconstruction rather than evaluating a sufficiently specified opposing alternative.

moves.attributionBasis: Carrier answers MacDonald's explicit question about Gnostic support, with only a brief agreement from MacDonald during the continuing response.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
moves.proposition: The early Q tradition portrays Jesus as a mortal Jewish reformer concerned with burdensome interpretations of law and modeled on figures regarded as historical, rather than as a preexistent savior.
moves.attributionBasis: MacDonald introduces his commitment to Q and develops the argument continuously through the final row before turning explicitly to Paul.

components.text: Whether the earliest recoverable Jesus was a preexistent celestial savior rather than a mortal figure.
Whether early evidence contains a nonrevelatory earthly placement of Jesus.

response.rationale: The Q portrait of a mortal law reformer directly contacts the celestial-model demand and supplies contrary early-tradition material, though it does not fully answer Pauline silence or establish Q’s independence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive celestial-versus-mortal component but leaves chronology, independence, and Pauline evidential expectations underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mortal-law-reformer claim and comparisons are clear, though the source-critical status of “the Q document” is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Q characterization supports a mortal portrait, but the inference from literary comparison to historicity needs an explicit source-critical caveat.

charity.alternative: Q could be a later literary or communal construction rather than independent memory of a mortal teacher.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Q’s concern with legal burdens, absence of preexistence language, and comparisons with Moses, Ezekiel, and Isaiah as mortal historical figures.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
moves.proposition: Paul's theology requires a mortal Jesus crucified in connection with a dispute over Jewish law, while Paul's focus on faith and resurrection explains his subsequent mythologizing and limited earthly biography.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person turn continues MacDonald's comparison of Q, Paul, mortality, and Jewish law.

components.text: Whether Paul’s crucified Jesus is better located among mortals or in a celestial firmament.
Whether Paul’s sparse earthly biography is unexpected if Jesus was historical.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both the location of crucifixion and the significance of Pauline silence by invoking mortality, law, and letter purpose, but it does not compare celestial crucifixion language in detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it reaches both decisive issues but compresses the textual and comparative warrants needed to defeat the con inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The law, crucifixion, and epistolary-purpose claims are clear, though the restriction of crucifixion to earthly mortals remains an unstated premise.

charity.decisiveQualification: Crucifixion language alone does not locate the death unless Pauline context excludes the proposed celestial setting.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the reply directly attacks the Pauline-silence inference and the positive celestial model.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly identifies the theological issue but largely assumes rather than defeats the celestial-location alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Christ’s death to the end of the law, calls crucifixion something happening to mortals, and explains Paul’s focus through faith and resurrection.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald

moves.attributionBasis: MacDonald explicitly addresses Carrier and develops his own reading of Antiquities 20, Josephus, James, and the law dispute.

components.text: Whether any source independent of the Gospels supplies external attestation for Jesus.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive no-external-evidence premise with a specific allegedly independent passage.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cited passage and proposed legal context are identifiable, though the conclusion assumes the transmitted wording and biological identification are reliable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The insistence that Josephus does discuss the relevant Jesus is stronger than warranted without addressing textual transmission and alternative kinship readings.

charity.alternative: The James wording may be nonbiological, misunderstood, or textually altered and thus fail to attest Jesus independently.
charity.decisiveQualification: The passage anchors Jesus only if its wording is authentic and identifies the Christian Jesus through ordinary kinship.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supplies the principal claimed external attestation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies the relevant passage but does not yet engage the strongest authenticity and identification qualifications.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
moves.proposition: Although Mark is heavily mythologized, its comparison of Jesus with mortal epic heroes makes sense as the literary elevation of an underlying mortal Jewish teacher into a superior hero.
moves.attributionBasis: MacDonald states agreement with Carrier's mimesis analysis, then supplies a clearly marked caveat grounded in his own published thesis.

components.text: Whether mythologically composed Gospel biography presupposes an underlying historical person.

response.rationale: The comparison with mortal epic heroes contacts the historical-substrate issue, but compatibility between mythologizing and historicity does not establish that Mark required a historical teacher.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive substrate question but leaves the inference from mortal comparands to an actual historical subject underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The literary-elevation thesis is recoverable, though “almost need” leaves the modal force and exact necessity claim somewhat implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mortal status of Hector and Odysseus shows literary comparability, but does not by itself make a historical Jesus nearly necessary.

charity.alternative: Mark could construct an earthly mortal hero from prior literary and theological materials without preserving a historical teacher.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mortal literary comparands do not themselves discriminate between transformation of history and fabrication of earthly biography.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Literary elevation is compatible with a historical substrate, but the claimed need for that substrate does not follow from mortal epic comparisons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific comparands and their mortality are supplied, while evidence linking Mark’s starting material to remembered biography is absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the mythic-transformation bridge and challenges wholesale Gospel fabrication.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes extensive mythmaking but does not address the strongest reification account’s decisive nondiscrimination point.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that Mark presents Jesus as superior to mortal Hector and Odysseus and frames this as elevation from Jewish teacher to epic hero.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
moves.proposition: First John's sensory-witness language and Papias's interest in living voices and named disciples constitute early testimony that a mythologized Jesus nevertheless existed and attracted identifiable followers.
moves.attributionBasis: MacDonald reads and interprets First John and Papias before explicitly summarizing this material as the substance of his response.

components.text: Whether identifiable early witness traditions provide corroboration beyond rewritten Gospel myth.
Whether later testimony can reliably establish the earliest historical situation.

response.rationale: The sensory-witness and named-follower material contacts the corroboration issue, but the excerpt does not establish independence, date, or transmission sufficient to overcome the source-limit demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it reaches the corroboration component but does not answer the decisive chronology and independence qualifications.

precisionFindings.rationale: The witness claim is clear, but First John, the Fourth Gospel, and Papias are grouped as early transmission without stable distinctions of date, genre, or dependence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Sensory rhetoric and interest in named voices are treated as valuable historical evidence without the necessary independence and genre qualifications.

charity.alternative: Sensory-witness rhetoric and named traditions may be literary claims transmitted within dependent communities rather than independent testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: The material corroborates historicity only if its source access and independence from Gospel tradition are defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it attacks the con claim that later witness traditions cannot provide secure independent evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move calls dismissal dogmatic but does not engage the strongest dependence and genre-based explanation of the evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes First John as evidence for Jesus and named admirers, describes Johannine transmission as faithful lore, and concedes Fourth Gospel mythologization.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Matthew's Mosaic Jesus can reify communal, scriptural, or revelatory teachings, so Mosaic mythologization does not require memories of a historical teacher.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier rejects the asserted oral tradition, agrees with the Mosaic literary pattern, and repeatedly contrasts two explanations of that pattern.

components.text: Whether Mosaic and legal teachings require memory of a mortal historical reformer.
Whether mythological elevation is better explained by transforming a historical person.

response.rationale: The reply directly offers communal, scriptural, and revelatory sources that can be reified as an earthly Mosaic teacher, answering the claimed need for historical memories without proving actual dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive necessity inference and explains an alternative mechanism, but does not document that mechanism in the relevant texts.

precisionFindings.rationale: Reification is clearly described as placing inherited teachings into an earthly Mosaic figure, with several possible source channels expressly preserved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims explanatory availability and parity rather than proof, appropriately acknowledging uncertainty about where the teachings originated.

charity.alternative: The teachings could preserve material from a mortal reformer subsequently modeled on Moses.
charity.decisiveQualification: Literary reification is compatible with historical input even if it shows that such input is not required.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances Gospel reification and attacks the early-mortal-tradition inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly allows multiple origins and limits its conclusion to both theories being able to explain the literary phenomenon.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains that teachings from revelation, scripture, or an original sect can be put into an earthly figure’s mouth using Moses as the model.

components.text: Whether Mark transforms a remembered mortal teacher rather than Pauline and other literary materials.

moves.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
moves.proposition: Overlaps between Paul and reconstructed Q, including kingdom-of-God and mission traditions, are better explained by shared tradition than by wholesale derivation of Gospel material from Paul.
moves.attributionBasis: MacDonald introduces examples from Paul and his Q reconstruction, lists their overlaps, and evaluates the proposed direction of dependence.

components.text: Whether Josephus’s James wording securely identifies a biological brother of the Christian Jesus.
